Q: When I hit Alt + Tab, VS Code auto-saves and formats code. How can I stop it? A:

There was a bug in VS Code which caused AutoSave to trigger editor.formatOnSave even when files.autoSave is set to afterDelay.

The March 2024 release includes the fix for this (release date: 4 April 2024).

Q: Water Solution keep getting error message "did not find 12\n" A:

Due to the length of time and the apparent upgrades to the CS50 library, the code, as is, would not compile anymore.

/home/craig/C_Programs/Console/CS50_Water/main.c|8|error: too few arguments to function ‘get_int’|

Input functions, such as "get_int" now require text to be used as a prompt.

int minutes = get_int("How many minutes do you shower for?\n");

With those bits of refactoring, rerunning the test provides the following output for one of the time prompts and a clue as to what the checker process is looking for.

craig@Vera:~/C_Programs/Console/CS50_Water/bin/Release$ ./CS50_Water 
How many minutes do you shower for?
5
Minutes: 5
Bottles: 60
5 minute equals 60 bottles.
 5

Usually, one wants the prompting with some validation as noted, to occur at the beginning of the program and not repeated after the program logic is executed. With that, following is a refactored version of the code that should reflect the spirit of the task.

int main(void)
{
    int minutes, bottles;

    do  /* Place the prompt here before the calculation     */
    {
        minutes = get_int("How many minutes do you shower for? ");
    }
    while (minutes < 0);

    bottles = minutes * (192/16);
    printf("Minutes: %i\n",minutes);
    printf("Bottles: %i\n",bottles);
    printf("%i minute equals %i bottles.\n", minutes, bottles);

    return 0;
}

Following were various tests that mimic the detail noted in the checker process.

craig@Vera:~/C_Programs/Console/CS50_Water/bin/Release$ ./CS50_Water 
How many minutes do you shower for? 1
Minutes: 1
Bottles: 12
1 minute equals 12 bottles.
craig@Vera:~/C_Programs/Console/CS50_Water/bin/Release$ ./CS50_Water 
How many minutes do you shower for? 2
Minutes: 2
Bottles: 24
2 minute equals 24 bottles.
craig@Vera:~/C_Programs/Console/CS50_Water/bin/Release$ ./CS50_Water 
How many minutes do you shower for? 5
Minutes: 5
Bottles: 60
5 minute equals 60 bottles.
craig@Vera:~/C_Programs/Console/CS50_Water/bin/Release$ ./CS50_Water 
How many minutes do you shower for? 10
Minutes: 10
Bottles: 120
10 minute equals 120 bottles.
craig@Vera:~/C_Programs/Console/CS50_Water/bin/Release$ ./CS50_Water 
How many minutes do you shower for? abc <-- note a request to retry when invalid data entered
How many minutes do you shower for? 2
Minutes: 2
Bottles: 24
2 minute equals 24 bottles.

The takeaway here would be to delve further into C tutorials regarding the use of "for" loops, "while" loops, and "do/while" loops.

Q: Enum vs Strongly typed enum A:

There's a good article about enums at this IBM page, it's very detailed and well-written. Here are some important points in a nutshell:

The scoped enums solve most of the limitations incurred by regular enums: complete type safety, well-defined underlying type, scope issues, and forward declaration.

  • You get type safety by disallowing all implicit conversions of scoped enums to other types.

  • You get a new scope, and the enum is not anymore in the enclosing scope, saving itself from name conflicts.

  • Scoped enums gives you the ability to specify the underlying type of the enumeration, and for scoped enums, it defaults to int if you choose not to specify it.

  • Any enum with a fixed underlying type can be forward declared.

Q: C++ printing to terminal much slower when adding g++'s -std=c++<##> flag? A:

The differences are solely due to the terminal. Both alternatives are writing to the terminal, which has to maintain scroll history and draw the pixels of the written characters. The terminal works much harder than the short benchmark that only spits out ASCII characters.

In fact, your terminal and/or OS are extremely slow. I have run the same program, compiled with gcc-8.2.0, on a MAC terminal, and it ran in 0.175374 seconds once, and 0.186559 another time. While I did not gather a significant amount of statistical data, I could not see any difference with and without -std=c++14.

It seems to be an issue with an extremely slow terminal that is more than 100 times slower than the MAC terminal, not with the code itself. Most likely, your terminal becomes slower when it gathers history, so the second time it runs, it gets slower, regardless of the compilation flags.

Edit after seeing the updated question:

It is possible that the default is -std=gnu++14, which performs some nonstandard optimization that makes the terminal run faster. When you pass -std=c++14, the GNU extension is turned off.

For reference, look at compiling with std c11.... According to it, -std=c++14 means that _GNU_SOURCE is no longer defined, and a different implementation of printf could be used.

Q: WinMerge recently changed its key combinations, so is there a way to configure its key assignments? A:

Because "Merge Mode": superuser.com/q/1647260 –

With the current versions of WinMerge, the File menu is different from the screenshot in the above reference. However, I still resolved the issue by pressing F9 to disable the Merge Mode.

Also notice that when Merge Mode is enabled, there should be a word "Merge" on the bottom of the window. See the following screenshot.

Q: How to use aggregate function in lucene query string? A:

Unlike HQL (and SQL), Lucene query syntax does not let you retrieve aggregates. However, you might be interested in a somewhat similar feature called faceting which lets you retrieve category counts for your query .
